scope: Exact prior authored sources, form descriptors and complete target-pool/order hashes for bounded repairs; not full catalogue language approval.

priorEntry.usage: Used mostly in the third person: 'cosa succede?', 'cos'è successo?'. Irregular: passato remoto successe, participio successo. In this sense it does not mean 'to succeed' (that is 'riuscire' or 'avere successo').

examples.it: Ieri mi è successa una cosa strana.
examples.en: Yesterday something strange happened to me.

examples.it: Se succederà qualcosa, ti chiamo subito.
examples.en: If anything happens, I'll call you right away.

priorPolicy.note: Sta succedendo focuses on something occurring now; succede can also report what usually happens.

priorEntry.en: to touch; to be someone's turn
priorEntry.usage: Spelling change: tocchi, tocchiamo, toccherò. With essere and an indirect object it means 'to be someone's turn' or 'to have to': 'tocca a me' (it's my turn), 'mi tocca lavorare' (I have to work).

examples.it: A chi tocca? Tocca a te.
examples.en: Whose turn is it? It's your turn.

examples.it: Mi è toccato pagare per tutti.
examples.en: I ended up having to pay for everyone.

priorPolicy.note: Touching can be sustained as contact; the direct object names what is touched.

priorEntry.usage: Impersonal verb used only in the third person singular: bisogna + infinitive (bisogna partire presto) or bisogna che + subjunctive. Not used with a personal subject: 'I need' is 'ho bisogno di'.

examples.en: You have to book in advance.
It should have been said earlier.

examples.it: Bisogna che tu venga con noi.
examples.en: You need to come with us.

priorPolicy.note: Bisogna expresses an impersonal necessity. Use the simple form before an infinitive; there is no personal subject to put into an ongoing-action drill.

simpleExamples.en: It is necessary to book in advance.

past.en: It was necessary to book in advance.

simpleExamples.en: It is necessary to leave early.

past.en: It was necessary to leave early.

simpleExamples.en: It is necessary to check the documents.

past.en: It was necessary to check the documents.

simpleExamples.en: It is necessary to wait one’s turn.

past.en: It was necessary to wait one’s turn.

answerFormsByVariant: A wish, polite request or hypothetical result

priorEntry.en: to collapse; to fall down; to slump
priorEntry.usage: Used for buildings and bridges collapsing, prices or morale plummeting, and people dropping from exhaustion ('crollare dal sonno', 'crollare sul divano'). Regular -are verb with essere.

examples.it: Il vecchio ponte è crollato dopo la piena.
examples.en: The old bridge collapsed after the flood.

examples.it: Ero così stanca che sono crollata sul letto vestita.
examples.en: I was so tired that I collapsed on the bed fully dressed.

examples.it: Se continuano così, i prezzi crolleranno entro l'anno.
examples.en: If things go on like this, prices will plummet within the year.

priorPolicy.note: In the sense “collapse physically”, stare + gerundio highlights this action while it is underway. Use the simple present for a routine or broader fact.

priorEntry.en: to take care of oneself; to get treatment; to care about
priorEntry.usage: 'Curarsi' means to treat one's illness or look after one's health ('curarsi con gli antibiotici'); 'curarsi di qualcosa/qualcuno' is more formal and means to bother about or look after. The transitive 'curare' means to treat, to cure or to edit (a book). Regular -are verb.

examples.it: Se non ti curi, la tosse peggiorerà.
examples.en: If you don't get treatment, the cough will get worse.

examples.it: Si è curato con rimedi naturali per un mese.
examples.en: He treated himself with natural remedies for a month.

examples.it: Non si cura di quello che pensa la gente.
examples.en: She doesn't care what people think.

priorPolicy.note: In the sense “seek treatment for oneself”, stare + gerundio highlights this action while it is underway. Use the simple present for a routine or broader fact.
